{{Short description|Law in rheology}}
In [[rheology]], '''Byerlee's law''', also known as '''Byerlee's friction law'''<ref>
{{cite book|author1=E. B. Burov|editor1-last=Watts|editor1-first=Anthony B.|title=Crust and Lithosphere Dynamics: Treatise on Geophysics|date=2010|publisher=Elsevier|isbn=9780444535726|page=100|chapter=Plate Rheology and Mechanics}}
</ref> concerns the [[shear stress]] (τ) required to slide one rock over another. The rocks have macroscopically flat surfaces, but the surfaces have small asperities that make them "rough." For a given experiment and at normal [[Stress (mechanics)|stress]]es (σ<sub>n</sub>) below about 2000 bars (200 MPa) the shear stress increases approximately linearly with the normal stress (τ = 0.85 σ<sub>n</sub>, where τ and σ<sub>n</sub> is in units of MPa) and is highly dependent on rock type and the character (roughness) of the surfaces, see [[Mohr-Coulomb friction law]]. Byerlee's law states that with increased normal stress the required shear stress continues to increase, but the ''rate'' of increase decreases (τ = 0.5 + 0.6σ<sub>n</sub>), where τ and σ<sub>n</sub> are in units of MPa, and becomes nearly independent of rock type.<ref name=Byerlee1978>
{{cite journal|last1=Byerlee|first1=James D.|title=Friction of Rocks|journal=Pure and Applied Geophysics|date=July 1978|volume=116|issue=4–5|pages=615–626|doi=10.1007/BF00876528|bibcode=1978PApGe.116..615B |s2cid=128666327 |issn=0033-4553}}<!--|accessdate=19 July 2014-->
</ref>

The law describes an important property of [[crust (geology)|crust]]al rock, and can be used to determine when slip along a [[geological fault]] takes place.

The law is named after the American geophysicist James Byerlee, who derived it experimentally in 1978.<ref name="Byerlee1978" /><ref>{{Citation |last=Allaby |first=Michael |chapter=Byerlee’s rule |date=2020-01-23 |title=A Dictionary of Geology and Earth Sciences |chapter-url=https://www.oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/acref/9780198839033.001.0001/acref-9780198839033-e-10111 |access-date=2024-11-28 |publisher=Oxford University Press |language=en |doi=10.1093/acref/9780198839033.001.0001/acref-9780198839033-e-10111 |isbn=978-0-19-883903-3}}</ref>
